# AES Top-Level Module Specification

## 1. Purpose

This module is the top-level AES hardware accelerator. It provides block cipher encryption and decryption for AES-128, AES-192, and AES-256. It is intended to be controlled by software through a memory-mapped register interface and may optionally use an externally supplied key rather than a software-written key.

The module must behave as a self-contained AES peripheral: it must accept configuration, key material, initialization vectors, and input data; perform the selected cipher operation; expose output data; report status; consume entropy when required; and raise alerts on detected faults.

## 2. Features

The module must support:

- AES-128, AES-192, and AES-256 encryption and decryption.
- The following block cipher modes:
  - Electronic Codebook (ECB)
  - Cipher Block Chaining (CBC)
  - Cipher Feedback mode with 128-bit segment size (CFB-128)
  - Output Feedback (OFB)
  - Counter (CTR)
- Software-controlled automatic or manual block operation.
- Input data pipelining: the next input block may be written while the previous block is still being processed.
- Output data backpressure in automatic mode.
- Software-triggered and automatic reseeding of internal pseudo-random number generators.
- Optional key sideload from an external key-management source.
- Life-cycle escalation response.
- Recoverable and fatal alert reporting.

## 3. Reset and Initialization

After reset, the module must perform an initialization sequence before it becomes operational:

- It must obtain entropy from the entropy distribution interface to seed its internal pseudo-random number generators.
- It must clear key, initialization vector, input data, and output data registers using pseudo-random data.
- It must not assert its idle indication until this initialization sequence has completed.

Because sensitive registers are cleared with pseudo-random data, software must not assume that these registers have any particular reset value.

## 4. Register Interface Behavior

The module must be accessible as a memory-mapped peripheral through a TileLink-UL bus interface.

### 4.1 Endianness

All multi-word data objects, including key words, initialization vector words, and data words, must be little-endian.

### 4.2 Key Registers

- Key registers must be write-only.
- Reads from key registers must not return key material.
- The key must be written as two shares.
- The actual key is the bitwise XOR of the two shares.
- All key words must be written at least once for the module to accept a new key.
- The order in which the key words are written is not significant.
- When the AES-192 option is disabled, selecting AES-192 as the key length must not be treated as a valid configuration.

### 4.3 Data and Output Registers

- Input data registers must be write-only.
- Output data registers must be read-only.
- Each 128-bit data block consists of four 32-bit words.
- For a block operation to begin automatically, all four input data words must have been written.
- For the module to continue after producing output, all four output data words must have been read, unless manual operation mode is selected.

### 4.4 Control and Trigger Writes

- The main control register must be shadowed.
- A configuration update through the shadowed control register must require two writes of the same value.
- When the module is busy, writes to the control register, key registers, and initialization vector registers must be ignored.
- The module must provide trigger controls for:
  - Starting a manual operation.
  - Requesting a manual reseed of the masking pseudo-random number generator.
  - Clearing key, initialization vector, and input data registers.
  - Clearing output data registers.

## 5. Cipher Operation

### 5.1 Automatic Operation

In the default automatic mode, the module must behave as follows:

- When the module is idle and all required key, initialization vector, and input data conditions are satisfied, it must automatically start processing the input data block.
- The module must not automatically start with a partially updated initialization vector.
- After processing begins, the module should accept the next input data block while the current block is still being processed.
- After a block is complete, output data must remain available until all output words have been read.
- If the module completes a block while the previous output block has not yet been fully read, it must stall and must not overwrite the unread output data.

### 5.2 Manual Operation

In manual operation mode:

- The module must not automatically start a block when new input data is written.
- The module must start a block only when the start trigger is set.
- The start trigger must self-clear once the operation has started.
- The module must not apply output backpressure.
- Output data may be overwritten even if the previous output has not been read.

### 5.3 Key Change and Decryption Preparation

After a new key is loaded:

- For encryption, or for CFB, OFB, and CTR modes, the module may begin data processing without additional key preparation.
- For ECB or CBC decryption, the module must first derive the decryption start key from the newly supplied key.
- During this preparation, the module must not begin processing the data block and must indicate that it is not ready for normal operation.
- Once the decryption key preparation has completed, the module must be able to switch between encryption and decryption without repeating this preparation for the same key.

### 5.4 Initialization Vector and Chaining Behavior

The initialization vector is used in CBC, CFB, OFB, and CTR modes.

- In ECB mode, the initialization vector must be ignored.
- The module must update the initialization vector registers as required by the selected cipher mode.
- In CBC encryption, the initialization vector must be updated with the ciphertext output.
- In CBC decryption, the initialization vector must be updated with the previous input ciphertext block.
- In CFB mode, the initialization vector must be updated with the ciphertext output.
- In OFB mode, the initialization vector must be updated with the cipher output before it is combined with the input data.
- In CTR mode, the initialization vector must be updated using the standard 128-bit counter increment, and the increment must be big-endian.

### 5.5 Partial Final Blocks in OFB and CTR Modes

In OFB and CTR modes, the final data block need not be a full 128 bits. The module must still process a full 128-bit block internally, but software may use any padding for the unused bytes. The module must not require the padding to have any particular value.

## 6. Key Sideload

The module must support using a key supplied from an external key-management source instead of from the register interface.

- When key sideload is selected, writes to the software key registers must be ignored.
- The actual key must be taken from the sideload input.
- The module must not expose the sideloaded key through the register interface.
- If the externally supplied key is not marked valid, the module must not begin an automatic operation that depends on that key.
- After using a sideloaded key, software must be able to trigger clearing of the key material inside the module.

## 7. Status and Idle Indication

The module must provide status information to software that includes at least:

- An idle indication.
- Whether the module is ready to accept a new input data block.
- Whether output data is available to be read.
- Whether a fatal fault has been detected.

The idle output must be asserted only when the module is not actively processing a block and is ready for new configuration, key, and initialization vector writes. It must be deasserted while the module is processing data, preparing a decryption key, or performing an initialization or clearing sequence.

## 8. Entropy and Reseeding Behavior

The module must request entropy from the entropy distribution interface for two purposes:

- Clearing sensitive registers with pseudo-random data.
- Refreshing the randomness used by the masking countermeasure.

### 8.1 Entropy Request Behavior

- The module must present at most one entropy request at a time.
- If both clearing-related and masking-related entropy requests are pending, the clearing-related request must be served first.
- Once an entropy request has been asserted, it must remain asserted until the entropy source acknowledges the request.
- The module must not complete an operation that requires entropy until the required entropy has been received.

### 8.2 Reseed Triggers

- The module must reseed the register-clearing pseudo-random number generator when software requests it and as required during initialization.
- The module must reseed the masking pseudo-random number generator:
  - Automatically after a new key is provided, if this behavior is enabled by configuration.
  - Automatically after a software-configurable number of processed blocks.
  - When software explicitly requests a reseed.

A compile-time option may disable masking reseed requests for side-channel evaluation setups. When this option is enabled, the module must not issue masking reseed requests.

## 9. Alerts and Fault Behavior

The module must provide two alert classes:

- A recoverable alert for recoverable error conditions.
- A fatal alert for faults that require reset before the module can be used again.

### 9.1 Fatal Fault Behavior

When a fatal fault is detected, the module must:

- Assert the fatal alert.
- Record the fatal fault condition in status.
- Stop processing data.
- Prevent further cipher operations.
- Remain in a locked state until reset.

Examples of conditions that must cause fatal alert behavior include control path state errors, integrity errors on protected control or configuration paths, and other unrecoverable internal faults.

### 9.2 Recoverable Fault Behavior

A recoverable alert must be generated for conditions that do not require the module to permanently lock up. Such conditions must be reported without requiring a module reset.

### 9.3 Alert Testing

The module must allow software to test each alert output through dedicated alert test controls. Setting a test control must cause the corresponding alert output to be exercised.

### 9.4 Life-Cycle Escalation

When the life-cycle escalation input is asserted, the module must stop normal operation and enter a secure error state. The module must not process further data blocks. The module must remain in this state until reset.

## 10. Security-Relevant Behavioral Requirements

- Secret key material must never be readable through the bus interface.
- Key, initialization vector, and data registers must be cleared with pseudo-random data, not with a constant value, when clearing is performed.
- If masking is enabled, the module must use randomized masking internally and must obtain fresh randomness from the entropy interface as required.
- If mask forcing is allowed by a compile-time option, the module must provide a control to force mask values to zero for side-channel evaluation.
- If mask forcing is not allowed, the corresponding control must have no effect.

## 11. Compile-Time Options

The module must be parameterizable to:

- Enable or disable AES-192 support.
- Enable or disable first-order masking of the cipher path.
- Select the type of S-Box implementation used.
- Insert a configurable delay before starting a manually triggered operation.
- Allow or disallow forcing masks to zero.
- Enable or disable masking reseed requests.
- Configure whether alert outputs are synchronous or asynchronous.

Selection of these options may change area, latency, entropy consumption, and side-channel resistance, but must not change the externally specified functional behavior described above.

## 12. Interface Expectations

The module must operate from a single main clock and reset.

All outputs driven by the module must be at known values after reset.

No interrupt output is required. Software must use status polling to determine readiness and completion.
